audience.programmeDescription: Landscape Architecture and Planning studies how people shape places for human and ecological needs. This Dutch-taught programme combines soil, water, ecology, geography and spatial evidence with planning and creative design. The example follows the Landscape Architecture specialisation.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR programmes respond through landscape processes and nature-based interventions, ecological and spatial investigation, or land-use governance and participation. WUR offers much more sustained landscape design, studio practice, planting, construction and representation. UCR’s Spatial Planning course supports geospatial environmental applications; it does not replace that professional training.

curriculum.limitation: This 180-credit example contains 96 common credits, 42 taught specialisation credits, a 12-credit design thesis and 30 open credits. It assumes VWO Mathematics A preparation and completes the required taught study and safety preparation before the thesis.

concepts: Combines landscape-forming processes, soil and water, ecology, GIS and nature-based interventions with social inquiry, visual analysis and policy. The emphasis is on understanding places and evaluating sustainable spatial responses.

Prioritises the ecological and physical evidence for landscape decisions: biodiversity, ecosystems, farming, soils, water, Earth observation, environmental chemistry, resource use and quantitative investigation.
Prioritises decisions about places: institutions, law, social differences, participation and communication, alongside GIS, nature-based adaptation, environmental governance and public economics.

notes.text: WUR combines landscape processes with repeated site, urban and regional design studios, planting, construction, representation, aesthetics and a research-based design thesis. UCR can address landscapes through substantial environmental and geospatial investigation, nature-based interventions, visual analysis and governance. The professional studio sequence, planting/construction detailing and design-thesis training remain major differences.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
